0.1 This

FOREWORD

Indian Standard ( Part VI ) was adopted by the Indian Standards Institution on 5 June 1980, after the draft finalized by the Environmental Testing Procedures Sectional Committee had been approved by the Electronics and Telecommunication Division Council. 0.2 This standard deals with guidance to hydrogen sulphide test for contacts and connections of electronic and electrical items. The hydrogen sulphide test is covered in IS : 9000 ( Part XXV )-1980*.

assistance is derived from Dot : 50B 0.3 In preparing this standard, ( Central Office ) 216 ' Draft-Guidance to Publication 68-2-43, Test Kd: Hydrogen sulphide test for contacts and connections ' issued by the lnternational Electrotechnical Commission. 0.4 For the purpose of deciding whether a particular requirement of this standard is complied with, the final value, observed or calculated, expressing the result of a test or analysis, shall be rounded off in accordance with IS : 2-196Ot. The number of significant places retained in the rounded off value should be the same as that of the specified value in this standard.

1. SCOPE 1.1 This standard ( Part VI ) contains guidance to the test intended to provide accelerated means to assess the effects of atmosphere, pol1ute.d with hydrogen sulphide, on the tarnishing of silver and silver alloys used for contacts and connections.

2.1 The test has been devised to assess the consequence of tarnishing of silver and some of its alloys. It has been largely validated by laboratory and field tests on silver, though limited tests have also been carried out on components with contacts of some silver alloys.
2.2 When .the same tarnish test is appropriate to test items containing different contact materials, then the test conditions may give rise to different accelerations ( see 8 ) and considerable experience and experimentation may be required to assess relative results. Contact alloys of . silver and palladium represent a case where the test is appropriate but where such care is required. 2.3 When the test is used for contacts and connections involving silver alloys and'silver in conjunction with other materials the test is expected to give more realistic results for those involving silver together with a more precious metal than it will for silver alloys ( or structures ) involving significant quantities of base metals. The following cases are given by way of example:

4

Gold contacts' are largely unaffected by the test; Contacts kvolving gold layers over silver or gold contacts in the close proximity of silver will be affected due to the phenomena sulphide. Both these effects are true of creeping silver reflections of field behaviour; and Copper and alloys containing high percentages of copper ( such as phosphor bronze or brass) are heavily tarnished in the test atmosphere due to the formation of copper sulphides. However, this type of tarnishing rarely predominates in practice, where oxide formation inhibits sulphide growth. Hence the test is behaviour is inappropriate in these cases, if the tarnishing required to resemble that occurring naturally.

3. APPLICABILITY

OF THE

TEST

3.1 This test provides accelerated means of assessing the effects of hydrogen sulphide containing atmosphere on contacts and connections. It is particularly useful as a comparative test. The relation between test values and service life is influenced by a large number of factors and can only be vaguely estimated after years of experience with this test in comparison with behaviour in the field. The test, therefore, cannot be expected to give a direct and exact determination of the actual service life of the tested contact or connection in any given natural atmosphere in practice. It is hardly necessary to state that the test is not suitable as a ' general corrosion test `, that is, to predict the corrosive behaviour of a given component in atmospheres, the major corrosive agent of which is other than hydrogen sulphide.
4

IS : 9001 (apart VI ) - 1980 3.2 On other hand, the test is very useful for checking the behaviour of production batches in comparison with the behaviour of `analogous components. In the course of time, other applications may be found for the test method. 4. INTRODUCTION 4.1 Satisfactory TO THE TEST

performance during the desired lifetime of contacts and connections depends on many parameters. Some of them determined by their design ( type, materials, forces, etc ) and others by the environment in which they have to function. Regarding the effects of the environment, special attention shall be paid to the polluting substances contained - usually in very small amounts - in the atmosphere. 4.2 Silver and some of its alloys are particularly susceptible to tarnishing by the minute quantities of hydrogen sulphide that occur in many The tarnish product is dark in colour and consists largely environments. of silver sulphide. Separable electrical connections employing these metals~as contact materials may therefore suffer from increased contact resistance and contact noise as a result.

5. HYDROGEN 5.1 Hydrogen

SULPHIDE

IN THE

ATMOSPHERE

sulphide is evolved by bacterial reduction of sulphates in vegetation, soil, stagnant water and animal waste. It is then oxidized through sulphur dioxide back to sulphates which are returned to the earth via precipitation for re-adsorption by living organisms. Hydrogen sulphide is more important in this natural sulphur cycle than sulphur dioxide, since it is the principal sulphur input, and also because it survives It is therefore a more widespread pollutant longer in t,he atmosphere. than sulphur dioxide. The latter is responsible for corrosion of a much wider range of materials but dominates only in urban areas, where it is produced largely by the burning of fossil fuels [see IS :, 9000 ( Part XXVI )-1980* 1. 5.2 Although the major input to the sulphur cycle is by hydrogen sulphide through natural processes, industrial processes also play a part. Oil refineries, chemical plants and gas works are all possible sources. Atmospheric concentrations of 1 to 30 ppb (parts in 10" by volume) are commonly reported. At many sites, peak values exceed this, and much higher concentrations are found close to sources. Other sulphurous Sulphur dioxide has little effect on pollutants are much less important. silver unless the concentration and humidity is high, and then it produces

The two commonest a tarnish product that is rarely found in practice. organic sulphurous pollutants, methyl mercaptan and carbon disulphide Some organic sulphur derivatives do tarnish do not tarnish silver at all. silver, as does elemental sulphur vapour, but these materials probably only occur in a small minority of environments. 6. TYPES

OF CONTACTS

AND CONNECTIONS

6.1 As this test is specifically intended for certain types of contacts and connections (other than those of the welded or soldered type ), a short description of these types of contacts and connections is considered to be useful.
6.2 Contacts and connections may be divided into two types and could In both cases, metal surfaces be described as permanent or temporary. are held together by an external force. 6.3 In the case of permanent connections, the force is very great and will usually cause permanent deformation of the metals and it is possible that a form of local welding takes place. Such connections are not intended to be made and broken during their lifetime. Examples of permanent connections are crimp and wrap joints. 6.4 With temporary connections, the force holding the metals in contact is, by comparison, light and they are of course designed to be made and broken possibly very many times during their lifetime. Examples of switches and relays. In temporary connections are: connectors, temporary connections the areas of metal which make contact with each other are in some cases referred to as contacts. 6.5 The contacts or contact areas in temporary connections wiil be made of various metals according to duty and application. Most metals - with the exception of precious metals - suffer from atmospheric corrosion. ~When contact materials corrode, The contact resistance increases. extensive use of precious metal contacts would be costly, so it is common in many applications to use precious metal alloys or coatings of precious metal or alloys over base metals for contact materials. 6.6 In the case of permanent joints, it is not normal to use precious metals and some general corrosion of external surfaces by hydrogen sulphide shall be expected. But, in a properly designed and made, crimp or wire wrap joint, corrosion does not occur between the contact However, in joints that surfaces due to the cold weld at high pressure. are poorly made or weakened as a result of thermal cycling, corrosive -gas will penetrate into those contact areas with a resultant increase in contact resistance. 6

IS : 9001 ( Part VI ) - 1980 7. PARAMETERS OF THE TEST

7.1 This test is for contacts and connections primarily made of silver and silver alloys ( see 6), and the criteria of success or failure adopted is that of contact resistance. The test conditions shall therefore produce a tarnish layer whose effect on contact resistance is similar to that of naturally grown layers. At the same time, the test shoulcl accelerate tarnish film growth. Unfortunately, these two requirements tend to be conflicting, since rapidly grown tarnish layers tend to be softer and less adherent than those grown naturally. A compromise shall be struck between acceleration ( achieved by increasing pollutant concentration and humidity ), and realistic contact resistance behaviour.
present test aims to use 7.2 The concentration and relative humidity contact resistance behaviour. 7.3 The major parameters the highest hydrogen sulphide that is compatible with realistic

of test are the following.

Hydro~qen Sulphide - Experience on silver 7.3.1 Concentraficn indicates that above 15 ppm, hydrogen sulphide deposits become In fact, the rate of tarnishing is not very sensitive unrealistically soft. to hydrogen sulphide concentration, so there is little advantage in using higher concentrations. Very low concentration may give rise to difficulties due to adsorption on the equipment walls and to strong dependencies on the The acceleration may also be too local air flow around the test items. low for some types of test items ( see 8 ). 7.3.2 Relatbe Humid@ -- The tarnish reaction is sensitive to quite small changes in humidity. Little corrosion will occur below 70 percent RH ( relative humidity ) while evidence suggests that above 85 percent RH, the rate of tarnishing increases rapidly, but the tarnish deposits formed are not at all typical of those found in practice. Spike-like growth off silver sulphide is observed, suggesting that capillary condensation may occur at 85 percent RH. For this reason, the humidity during the entire test shall be carefully controlled between the limits specified. Any of the known methods for determination of relative humidity may be used, provided that they measure the specified tolerances with sufficient Wet and dry bulb methods have been found satisfactory. accuracy. 7.3.3 Temperature -At temperatures above 3O"C, there is again a tendency for the nature of the corrosion mechanism to change, while at the test-time would unduly increase. The lower temperatures temperature of 25�C f 2�C is the most satisfactory compromise. Close control of temperature is necessary to enable the relative humidity to be held within the specified limits. 7

nf

IS :9001( Part VI) - 1980 7.3.4 Flow Rate -A continuous flow of gas through the test cabinet is used so that the concentration of hydrogen sulphide is maintained constant, and is not depleted as the gas is taken up by the adsorbing surfaces inside A relative velocity within specified limits is required the test cabinet. between the atmosphere and the test items and is obtained by moving the This is to avoid items or stirring the atmosphere in the test chamber. local depletion within the test chamber due to stationary air pockets. Reasonable care shall be taken to ensure that air flow may take place around test items in the cabinet, and also to ensure that the cabinet is not overpacked. All these precautions are necessary in order to ensure that all items are given uniform treatment throughout the test period.
7.35 Test Duration - The tarnishing brought about by exposure to the test atmosphere and the degradation of the tested contacts increase with the duration of the exposure, although the increase will generally not be Nevertheless, different severities of proportional to the time of exposure. the test may be obtained by lengthening the time of exposure, as set out in 8. 7.3.6 Illumination-It is known that silver tarnishes faster in bright For this reason a level of illumination than it does in darkness. illumination is specified in the test. This level has been chosen so that it may be attained inside an acrylic resin test cabinet ( sited away from direct daylight ) using normal room lighting. 7.3.7 Control of Test Conditions -- A close control of test conditions is required in order to assure reproducible results; of special importance are control of relative humidity ( see 7.3.2 ) and temperature ( see 7.3.3 ). A continuous or frequent monitoring of test conditions is desirable to ensure that the test parameters are maintained throughout the whole of the test period. 8. SEVERITY

OF THE TEST

8.1 It is, in principle, impossible to attach a unique acceleration factor to the test conditions. This is because the acceleration produced depends on the construction and materials present in the test items, and their conditions of use. Some general guidance based on experience to date is given here. This guidance should become more complete as experience with the test grows.
8.2 The following a test, or choosing considerations apply when assessing the the test duration appropriate to a particular results case. of

8.2.1 If a contact surface is not shielded or enclosed, and if it is exposed to a circulating atmosphere, then increasing the concentration of hydrogen sulphide in the atmosphere may have a relatively small 8

IS : 9001 ( Part VI ) - 1980 Increasing from 10 parts in 10' ( which effect on its rate of tarnishing. may occur naturally ) to 15 parts in lo8 ( the test concentration) has been found to increase the rate of tarnishing by a factor of 10 or less. 8.2.2 The contacts inside most practical test items are normally partially enclosed or shielded by the structure of the component or sub-assembly. At the very low concentrations of hydrogen sulphide that occur naturally, the rate of tarnishing is then limited by the mass transport of the pollutant through the atmosphere to the contact ( that is, the hydrogen sulphide concentration adjacent to the contact surface is lower than that in the atmosphere surrounding the test item ). 8.2.3 The effect of partially enclosing or shielding the contact surfaces against the test atmosphere is however very much less, due to the higher pollutant concentration. 8.2.4 The acceleration produced in the test is, as relatively low for test items containing unshielded contacts items would tarnish rapidly in real atmospheres containing in log of hydrogen sulphide. The acceleration is however for test items containing partially enclosed or shielded these would tarnish at a slower rate in field environments. 9. EVALUATION OF RESULTS noted earlier, because such a few parts much higher contacts, since

9.1 The main criterion of performance in this test is change of contact resistance while visual appearance is of secondary importance. It shall be remembered that most metals and alloys - for which this test is designed - will tarnish in the test and such corrosion shall be expected. Performance will be judged on the change in contact resistance. 9.2 When testing permanent connections of the crimp or wire wrap type, it is the change of resistance of the joint which is to be measured. If there is a significant increase in contact resistance, it is because the joint was not gas-tight and it was a poor joint. 9.3 When testing temporary connections, the contacts may be exposed in Mated contacts shall be measured at the mated or un-mated condition. the end of the exposure period without being disturbed while un-mated contacts shall be mated once only and measured. 9.4 The method used for measuring the contact resistance will be stated in the relevant specification. As the contacts for which this test is primarily designed are those intended to carry small current low voltage signals, it is necessary to use a low voltage low current measurement method ( Max 20 mV, 50 mA ) in order not to destroy films of corrosion products which may have formed. 9
